3.ask: Do one five-minute tending act on something you've been neglecting and tell one person you did it.
3.core:
There's something you were tending, and the habit fell out of your hands. You can probably picture what it looked like when you checked on it daily; not much past that. The skill is still there, but the using of it stopped, and the gap got wider the longer you didn't step back in.

What's empty isn't the ability. It's the contact. You don't need a big plan, just one small piece back in your palms, and someone who hears about it. Do the small act and say so; don't promise anyone a garden. Fifteen minutes at the edge of it is enough to put your hands back where they were.
3.sheetLine: You know how. You just stopped doing it.

4.tense: You are already tending something through a season it cannot skip, and you call it waiting for the right time.
4.verb: learning by tending and letting what grows set the pace
4.place: where the next step is visible and the road isn't
4.ask: Name the stage your thing is actually in, out loud, in your own words, to someone who's seen it.
4.core:
You keep saying you're waiting for the right time, but the care is already underway; it's just happening under a name that hides it. Small daily adjustments, checking on what you can't see yet, choosing not to force it. That's attention with a purpose, and it's been running for a while without you calling it that.

When you do a thing without owning it, you lose track of what you've actually built, and you can't ask for help without telling the story wrong. Say what this is. Say what stage it's in. You don't have to claim it's working or that it will. Just stop calling your own patient attention a delay.
4.sheetLine: The care is already running. You keep calling it waiting.

1.tense: You're tending something and it's working because you're actually there while it happens.
1.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them
1.place: Standing where who you are is becoming visible
1.ask: Let one thing that's growing near you reach done without reaching for the next. Notice what's left in your hands.
1.core:
You're tending something and it's growing on you — well, it is growing, and not because you're forcing it. You water it, you check the leaves, you let it get on with what it does. This is steady apprenticeship, keeping watch over something that isn't finished yet.

Becoming who you are shows up as this doing. Not a decision you'll make later, not some later claiming of yourself, but the ordinary hands-on care that anyone nearby can watch you give. Care that doesn't exhaust itself is rare, so notice when it isn't draining you. The moment something is done and you're still fussing over it, that's the only place to look. What you're doing is already you, and letting go of one finished thing is where the next of you shows up.
1.sheetLine: You're tending it well — notice that.

2.tense: Before anything has a chance to be, you're already watering what might happen next week.
2.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them
2.place: Standing where who you are is becoming visible
2.ask: Stop one task before it needs you again. Do something with no use to the project at all, and let that stand for the day.
2.core:
You see the finished shape before it's here and you're getting everything ready early, asking people if they've handled their part, fixing what isn't broken yet.

That push comes from real care, but it's a check on a season that hasn't started, and it misses the person sitting in front of you now. The thing you're dreaming of is a good one. It just hasn't finished cooking, and worry can't hurry something that grows at its own pace. Letting the future arrive on its own schedule isn't giving up on it. Your hands can be busy being useful. They don't have to be holding tomorrow too.
2.sheetLine: You're pouring water on a season that hasn't arrived.

3.tense: You're standing past a doorway where your own hands went quiet, and the quiet is still around you.
3.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them
3.place: Standing where who you are is becoming visible
3.ask: Pick the smallest living thing you've been upkeeping — the plant, the pot by the sink — and give it ten real minutes today.
3.core:
The plant on the sill has been getting by. A neighbor's garden looks tended, and yours looks like it's waiting for you to come back to it. You can see what wants water. It just isn't reaching your hands yet.

Most of what you've been keeping going has been kept from a distance, and that distance has become normal. The move back is tiny. It isn't about fixing your whole grip on things, and it doesn't ask you to feel like a gardener first. One small living thing, given ten real minutes by you, gets your hands moving again. Picking up the watering can is enough to start.
3.sheetLine: You pulled your hands back. The growing didn't leave.

4.tense: You're already the one shaping this — you just call it the situation needing you.
4.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them
4.place: Standing where who you are is becoming visible
4.ask: Name one bit of upkeep you do and say plainly who keeps it going. Say it out loud to yourself once.
4.core:
The little fixes, the reminders, the quiet arranging that keeps something alive: that's you being who you are, and you're describing it like it happened on its own. The upkeep runs fine, but the credit is going to nobody.

Becoming who you are needs you to see whose hands are doing it. Not as praise, not as a big word — just accurate. When you file your own steady care under 'it just needed doing', the next version of you has no address to arrive at. Claiming what you keep alive covers what's actually in your hands, not the whole story of who you've been. One true sentence about your own upkeep is enough to put the pen back in your hand.
4.sheetLine: You're doing the upkeep. You just haven't claimed it.

1.tense: The person is tending a thing and seeing the whole pattern of it at the same time.
1.verb: tending something material and watching how it actually grows
1.place: seeing the whole pattern from inside
1.ask: Name what the thing you're tending is turning into, then step back and leave it be for a week to turn into that by itself.
1.core:
You look after something and you can tell what it's becoming. Not only the daily upkeep — the full shape, where it started, how far it's come, where it's still going. Most people stand too close to their own work for that. You don't.

Care and clear sight work as a pair here. You're patient with the timing, careful with the thing, and you can also stand back and take in the whole of it, which is what makes your care land. You've built some of this already. You can also tell it's time to trust the thing a little more than your hands. What comes next isn't finishing it. It's letting what you've made stand on its own and watching that with the attention you've been giving the making. That part is harder, and it's still yours.
1.sheetLine: You tend it and you see the whole shape of it.

2.tense: The person will keep pushing the thing toward a version it isn't ready for yet.
2.verb: tending something material and watching how it actually grows
2.place: seeing the whole pattern from inside
2.ask: Write down the stage the thing is actually in right now, then leave it untouched for one day.
2.core:
You can already make out what this turns into, and past today there's a finished shape of it, working. So your hands keep moving toward that one — more than the thing can hold yet, more than it needs from you yet. Every check turns into a nudge.

Making out the whole pattern isn't the trouble. Aiming the whole pattern at the small thing you're tending is what's costing you. Care that clutches stops anything from growing, including you. The picture is safe in your hands. The thing in front of you is further back along that path than the picture is, and it needs the kind of attention that will let it sit still a while. It's noticing where the thing is now, not where it will be. That's a different pair of eyes, and you have them.
2.sheetLine: You're looking at where it's going, not where it is.

3.tense: The person has been tending things while stopping short of the whole pattern.
3.verb: tending something material and watching how it actually grows
3.place: seeing the whole pattern from inside
3.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and write what it's grown into from its start to today, keeping the question open as you go.
3.core:
You're tending things. You water what's in front of you, you sort what's in front of you, and the longer view doesn't arrive, so each day stands alone. The care is here. What would let it add up isn't, and it's been that way a while.

Looking clearly at what's right in front of you is the same ability as looking clearly at a whole life. Yours stops at the near edge, and you've had your reasons, which are yours and not for anyone else to name. What's missing is a second pair of eyes on your own work — the ones that say this has grown this far. Without it the hands keep moving and nothing settles. That's the part running low. Charge something that belongs to you instead, something that's yours to look at from your own center.
3.sheetLine: You tend what's in front of you and the whole shape stays dark.

4.tense: The person is already reading the whole course of a thing and calling it just following the steps.
4.verb: tending something material and watching how it actually grows
4.place: seeing the whole pattern from inside
4.ask: Say out loud that you saw what this needed and did it, about one recent move, with no explanation after.
4.core:
You can already tell how a thing develops — where it started, what it needs next, which parts to leave alone. You read that straight off the thing, and you act on it before anyone says what to do. Then you describe it as though the thing were deciding everything and you were keeping up.

What you read is real and it's been running a long time. The name you give it isn't. You've set the pace more than once in a way that doesn't call attention to itself, and keeping it unnamed is what makes the caring tiring — you carry all of it and take credit for none of what you decided. It's saying that the reading was yours, out loud, once. Anyone watching would say the moving was yours anyway.
4.sheetLine: You're reading the whole pattern already, just not saying so.

1.tense: You are here at the table with the pen, past the part where you had to prove the thing could grow.
1.verb: learning how things grow by tending them
1.place: the threshold where work is finished and becomes something else
1.ask: Name what you've made. Say it out loud in the room where you made it, once, and then let the next hour belong to something else.
1.core:
You've been tending something and it's grown. Not perfectly, but enough that you can see the shape of it now — the way the work has settled into a form that holds. You're not forcing it anymore. The care isn't wearing you down the way it did early on, when you had to check on it every few hours to believe it was still alive.

What's left isn't more tending. It's naming what's here. The next thing will come from that naming — not from you deciding what it should be, but from the finished thing making its own case. You've been holding it open a little longer than it needs. Not because it's unfinished, but because letting it be done feels like losing it.
1.sheetLine: You've grown the thing. You can put it down and still have it.

2.tense: You are already living in tomorrow's version of this, where it finally works, and you're bracing for the proof.
2.verb: learning how things grow by tending them
2.place: the threshold where work is finished and becomes something else
2.ask: Pick one thing you're growing and let it be what it is today. Don't adjust it. Notice what's still alive in it without your hands on it.
2.core:
You're ahead of where this actually is. Somewhere in your head there's a finished version — the thing grown, the point proven, the people in your life seeing what you knew it could be — and you're spending your days rushing toward that picture. Each choice gets read against whether it's getting you there.

So the work has turned into forcing. You're pushing the thing to grow faster than it's ready to, and pushing when nobody asked. You're at it more than it needs, which means you can't see what it actually needs from where you're standing — three months out, waiting for it to catch up. You haven't stopped caring. You've started gripping.
2.sheetLine: You're pushing it to grow toward a picture it hasn't drawn yet.

3.tense: You are standing at a door that closed behind you, still not walking through it.
3.verb: learning how things grow by tending them
3.place: the threshold where work is finished and becomes something else
3.ask: Do one small physical thing with what you've made this week — put it somewhere it can be seen, tell one person it exists, open the file and read it once.
3.core:
Something got finished, or nearly finished, and instead of turning toward what came next you stepped away and haven't stepped back. You can still see the shape of what you made from where you're standing, but it's behind glass. You describe it like something you used to do.

You know how to grow things. That part didn't leave. What's quiet is the warmth that used to come from working on something — and the less you do it, the quieter it gets. It doesn't come back by deciding to feel it. It comes back by doing one small piece of the work, badly, today, and letting the feeling catch up later if it wants to.
3.sheetLine: You stopped showing up to the work and the warmth went quiet.

4.tense: You are already in the room where the thing gets released, moving pen across paper you haven't acknowledged writing.
4.verb: learning how things grow by tending them
4.place: the threshold where work is finished and becomes something else
4.ask: Pick one thing you finished and say, out loud or in writing, 'I made this.' Then pick one thing still in your hands and say 'this isn't mine to carry.'
4.core:
You are already doing the work that comes after finishing — handing things off, moving the finished thing from the workbench to the shelf, turning toward what's next. But your stuff, your workload, the things you've built, your part in them, all get described as if someone else were keeping the operation running. You really are passing things along. What you're not doing is putting your name on it.

What you've been calling the situation is you, in the middle of a pass you've done many times before. You know how to finish things. You know the moment when pushing is done and handing off is the next move. What hasn't been said out loud is that this is what you do — which is why it keeps feeling like a problem you're managing instead of a thing you're choosing.
4.sheetLine: You're already passing things along. Say it's you doing it.
